headline: Cabinet Approves Fairfax's ₹52,878-Crore Bid for Controlling Stake in IDBI Bank
subheadline: Fairfax will acquire 60.72% of IDBI Bank from the government and LIC in what New Delhi calls the largest FDI ever in India's financial sector, subject to RBI clearance.
body:
• The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs has approved Fairfax Financial Holdings as strategic buyer of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank for ₹52,877.07 crore.
  • The stake combines the government's 30.48% and LIC's 30.24%; afterwards the government retains 15% and LIC 19%, a combined 34%.
  • The government says the deal, once completed, will be the largest FDI ever in India's financial sector.
  • Completion still requires Fairfax to present its credentials to the RBI under the fit-and-proper assessment and submit a compliance roadmap.

India's Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has approved the sale of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank to Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings for ₹52,877.07 crore, the Finance Ministry said in a statement reported by The Hindu BusinessLine. The buyer named in the approval is 10955230 Canada Inc, whose parent is Fairfax.

The government described the move as a strategic restructuring of IDBI Bank and said that, once completed, it will be the largest foreign direct investment in India's financial sector so far. It is also the country's biggest strategic disinvestment since Air India, according to BusinessLine's reporting of the decision. The original candidate report was carried by The Hindu.

How the stake is split

The 60.72% being sold comes from the bank's two large holders in equal-ish parts: 30.48% held by the Government of India and 30.24% held by the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC). Management control passes to Fairfax with the stake.

Neither seller exits fully. The government will retain a 15% residual holding and LIC will hold 19%, leaving them with a combined 34% in the restructured bank. Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw briefed reporters on the decision and the retained stake.

The Cabinet has also delegated authority to the Alternative Mechanism — the empowered ministerial group for disinvestment — to sell the government's residual 15% through the open market under the standard procedure. LIC, by contrast, will be free to manage its residual shareholding under its own internal procedures, subject to its regulators' directions.

A long process, a competitive field

The approval caps a process that has stretched over several years. Of five parties that initially submitted expressions of interest, four qualified under the eligibility and disqualification conditions, and two went on to submit techno-financial bids and become qualified bidders, the ministry said. It did not name the other bidder.

The ministry also stressed that there was no predetermined benchmark price: bidders valued the bank independently and submitted confidential sealed bids, while independent agencies valued the enterprise to judge whether the bids were reasonable.

What still has to happen

Cabinet approval is not completion. Fairfax must present its credentials to the Reserve Bank of India in line with the fit-and-proper assessment carried out at the expression-of-interest stage, and submit a roadmap for meeting the regulatory conditions attached to that assessment.

For depositors and borrowers, nothing changes on day one: the bank continues under its existing name and operations while the transaction moves through regulatory steps. For investors, the signal is larger — a global financial group taking control of a major Indian lender, with the state stepping back to a minority role, marks the most ambitious bank privatisation India has approved to date.
